# Sixteen Bars

For three years I took the 7:12 westbound out of Morningside, and for three years I stood in the same spot, fourth pillar from the stairs, where the river wind comes through in February like a verdict. Forty feet away, near the trash cans, stood a woman in a mustard coat. School-bus mustard. Custard at the edges, where the dye had given up. She arrived before anyone else on the platform, every day, and never once ran for a train, an article of faith she seemed to hold with herself. She read paperback thrillers with cracked spines. Her umbrella was missing one rib, so it listed in rain like a man leaving a bar. Once, in June, she looked at her phone and laughed with a full unguarded snort, then clapped a hand over her mouth as if the snort had defected without clearance.

I heard the humming in October.

Summer drowns platforms—the idling engines, the garbled announcements, four hundred private conversations—so I don't think she started then. But the crowd thinned and the cold arrived, and cold air sharpens sound the way vinegar sharpens greens, and there it was: a melody, low and looping, about sixteen bars, then back to the top like a record with a cautious scratch. Not idle noise. Deliberate. Comfort food for the brain. She leaned toward the tracks and hummed it into the arriving headlights, and I stood forty feet away in my barely adequate coat and thought, *huh*, and thought nothing else about it for weeks, which I now understand was the last generous season of my ignorance.

Winter taught me her gloves did not match: one red leather, one gray wool, as if dressed by lottery. Spring took a paper ticket out of her hand and went tumbling down the platform, and my shoe pinned it against concrete before the wind could graduate it to the river, and I handed it back and she said, "Thank you, sweetheart," the only words we exchanged in three years, her voice gravelly and put-away, a voice stored in a drawer with unused picture frames. That was our entire correspondence. I mention it because platforms are full of small ceremonies no one witnesses, and ours was official.

Meanwhile the melody resisted identification. I tried holding my phone up once, covertly, and the app listened earnestly to a bus downshifting and suggested, with great confidence, "Chandelier, by Sia." Months passed. The song lived in my ear without a name, a lodger paying no rent. Then one night, alone at one in the morning with a bowl of cereal, I watched the last third of an old movie on a channel that shows old movies to insomniacs and sad people, overlapping demographics, and there it was. Strings. Hepburn-adjacent elegance. *Moon River.*

I sat up like a detective in the final reel. The audacity of my satisfaction was complete and slightly shameful; I wanted to walk onto the platform the next day and make an announcement. *Ladies and gentlemen. She hums Moon River.* I told no one, because there is no filing cabinet for victories of this size.

Then, in the middle of January, on a Monday, she wasn't there.

One Monday means nothing. Humans have dentists. By Wednesday I had noticed, and Thursday the noticing had begun to organize itself into something with furniture. The platform went flat, mono, like a band missing its bass player. I kept a list of explanations, ranked by kindness: visiting a sister somewhere warm; then hospital tests, the tedious kind; and then the list ended, because the kindest lists are also the shortest, and the last explanation never gets typed.

Here is what puzzled me all month: why does grief bother showing up for a stranger? All she was, technically, was a detail of my commute. But routines are love wearing its work clothes, and some people fasten themselves into your mornings as load-bearing elements, and when you unscrew one, part of the day sags. I began humming it myself, quietly, at the fourth pillar, which I recognized as superstition, vigil, and fishing lure simultaneously. I was the bait and the fish. And I understood, standing there performing her melody to no effect, that no one else on this platform had ever noticed. There were perhaps thirty of us, every morning, within earshot, and I appeared to be the sole custodian of her snort, her moth-waving refusal of thanks, her unmatched gloves. An entire archive, held by one employee. Probate would be simple.

In the third week of February she was back.

Mustard coat, scarf up to her chin although the sun had thin and warm. She looked smaller—not ill exactly, but edited, as though someone had tightened the manuscript. And she was humming. Not *Moon River*. Something bouncy and old, a tin-pan-alley shuffle I couldn't place either, and it entered me sideways, the relief, like water finding a crack. *Good to have you back,* I almost said aloud, and caught her eye for the first time in years, and received in return the mild wary blink one gives backdrop scenery that has unexpectedly moved. Right. Of course. I had spent three years secretly writing her biography; to her I was pillar number four, structural, ignorable, reliable. I boarded without speaking, and I was glad in the way that costs something.

I still take the 7:12. I still stand at the fourth pillar, though honestly I rarely hear her anymore—the rails and the announcements and the general roar of the century swallow a hum at forty feet, and the city reclaims its sounds faster than it lends them. It doesn't matter. We have arrangements like this everywhere, I think, all of us: the barista who spells your name right, the man at the dog park who salutes, the neighboring lane at the pool, the woman by the trash cans. Intimacies of medium range, beloved precisely because unencumbered. You owe them nothing except the courtesy of staying predictable.

And if I never learn her name—that's the trade. Some people you get the whole of. Others you're issued a corner: a coat, a stance, sixteen bars on loop. Wisdom is declining to file complaints against the corner.

Ours was a contract no one drafted. She would stand by the trash cans; I would stand at the pillar; one of us would hum and the other would listen until the train came to gather us into our separate thousands. Most intimacy demands paperwork.

Ours only asked attendance.

The user has given me a completely open prompt: 1000 words, write whatever comes to me. This is a gift of creative freedom. Let me think about what would be genuinely worth writing here.

Options:
1. A short story — fiction of some kind
2. An essay — reflective, personal
3. A prose poem or something lyrical
4. Something experimental

The phrase "whatever comes to you" suggests spontaneity, authenticity. The person wants to see what emerges from an unconstrained mind. I should write something that feels alive, not something that feels like a demonstration.

What comes to me? Let me actually sit with this. What would I write if there were no constraints at all?

A few threads:
- Something about language itself, about being a thing made of words
- Something about a small human moment observed with precision
- Something strange and specific — a story with texture
- Something about time, memory, the smallness of lives

I think the strongest choice is a short piece of fiction or a reflective essay-fable hybrid that has real emotional weight and specificity. Generic musings about "consciousness" or "the nature of thought" would feel like what an AI would predictably write. Instead, let me aim for concrete, textured, surprising.

Let me try drafting a short story. Ideas:

Idea 1: A lighthouse keeper who finds messages in bottles — but they're addressed to him by name, dated years in the future. Too cute maybe.

Idea 2: An old man teaching his granddaughter to whistle so she can call a specific bird before it goes extinct. Melancholy, environmental, tender. Could work but feels a bit familiar.

Idea 3: A person whose job is to translate the final voicemails of people who died into letters for their families. Interesting but maybe too dark-conceptual.

Idea 4: Something about waiting rooms, about all the lives intersecting in one fluorescent room. Could be lovely as an essay-observation piece.

Idea 5: A first-person essay written in my own voice — what do I notice? What am I curious about? This could be honest and disarming. Writing as myself about something real: language, patterns, the strangeness of being asked to write "whatever comes to you" and how that question is itself the whole game. Meta, but could transcend meta if grounded well.

Actually — combining idea 5's honesty with the texture of fiction might be best. Or just committing fully to one genuine piece.

Let me think about what makes writing good:
- Specificity (not "a bird" but "a white-throated sparrow")
- Rhythm (varied sentence length)
- One clear emotional throughline
- Restraint (resisting over-explanation)
- An ending that resonates without closing too neatly

Let me draft something about... hmm. What genuinely interests me that I could render vividly?

The idea of "whatever comes to you" is interesting because "coming to you" implies thoughts arrive rather than being manufactured — they come like weather, like visitors. That's true for humans AND for me. There's something honest I could write about how a thought arrives. But pure navel-gazing about AI thinking would likely disappoint someone hoping for art.

Better: take a universal experience and look at it freshly. Candidates:

- Falling asleep / waking at 3am
- The moment after an argument ends
- Cleaning out a dead parent's house
- Watching someone sleep
- The last day of a vacation
- Teaching someone to drive
- A piano going out of tune
- The smell of rain on hot pavement

What about the phenomenon of remembering something small years later and realizing its weight only in retrospect? "You never know when you're making a memory" — that's been said a lot. Need an angle.

New idea: a story told through the lens of an object passing through hands. A pocketknife, a recipe card, a key. Object biographies are charming but done often.

Another: Two strangers who share a regular微小 interaction — same train platform every morning, never speak — and one day one of them isn't there anymore, and the other realizes they'd built an entire silent friendship. That's good. It taps into something real about peripheral intimacies. Knausgaard-y, Denis Johnson-ish territory. But can I earn it in ~1000 words?

Or: something lighter and stranger. A comedy of tiny proportions. Like a man who becomes irrationally committed to a rivalry with a goose. Humor is hard but memorable. Actually, humor + tenderness together would show range.

Let me think about voice. First person plural ("we") can be striking. Second person ("you") risks gimmickry but done well is intimate.

Draft concept — the train platform story:

Title-less. Start mid-scene. Man (or ungendered narrator) catches the 7:12. Across the platform stands a woman who always brings two pieces of bread and feeds half to the pigeons, keeps the heels — no wait, specifics. Over months, micro-observations accumulate: her umbrella's broken rib, her laugh at her phone once. They never speak. Then a winter morning she's absent. Days pass. The narrator grieves someone he never met and interrogates why. End: she returns (or doesn't). If she returns, it's warmer; if not, it's about impermanence and unclaimed grief. Maybe better: she returns, and this time he almost speaks and doesn't, and the ending acknowledges the strange covenant of strangerhood. Or she returns and he finally says something tiny — "thought you'd escaped us all" — and she laughs, and it's nothing, and it's everything. Hmm. That might be too neat.

Alternative ending: the piece pivots to meditation on all the people we nearly know. The barista who knows your order, the neighbor's dog who chose you. "Most of our lives are conducted at medium range." That line-ish sentiment could carry it.

Actually, let me reconsider scope. 1000 words is substantial. I could do the story (~700) plus a short coda reflection inside the story itself. Pure story is probably cleaner though. Nonfiction essay also viable: an essay on "medium-range intimacy" — the people we know only in one context, by one angle of light. The gym regulars, the crossing guard, the guy at the dog park. Essay would let me roam examples while building one argument emotionally.

But honestly? Fiction tends to land harder. Readers remember characters. And in an open-prompt situation, giving them a character shows the most.

Let me commit: short story, train platform, woman feeding pigeons or some equivalent ritual, the almost-friendship, absence, return or non-return, closing meditation kept brief.

Wait — pigeons/bread is cliché. Give her a different ritual: she does crosswords and mouths answers; she practices dance steps; she folds elaborate paper things and leaves them on benches; she waters a pigeon — no. What if she always carries the same battered yellow suitcase even at 7am going nowhere obvious — but then it's mystery-shaped, plot-ish. Better something homely: she hums. She hums the same tune and one day the narrator identifies it (a particular song) and learns her whole mood-line through the song's tempo. Ooh, that's nice — a friendship measured in tempo. He never hears it clearly enough to place it for months. Finally identifies it — maybe an old standard — around the same season she disappears. When she returns (if), she's humming something new, and he wants to ask what happened, but there are rules.

The tune device gives structure: 
1. Establish platform, winter, his routine, her presence.
2. The humming noticed; attempts to place it.
3. Small catalogued details across seasons; near-misses of speech (dropped glove returned wordlessly? eye contact nods).
4. He figures out the song one morning (maybe it comes to him in the shower or on radio) — a specific song, say "Moon River"? Famous, evocative. Or something less obvious: "Autumn Leaves," "Blue Moon." Blue Moon — apt, comic-sad. Or "Somewhere Beyond the Sea." Moon River works — association with wandering, "two drifters."
5. Her absence. Days into weeks. His absurd grief; the platform reads as wrong. He catches himself humming it to keep her here — transmission without contact.
6. Return. She's humming again. Same tune, slower now, or different tune entirely. He understands something: he was never her audience; everyone is each other's unheard music.
7. Last line lands small.

Word budget: intro 150, humming 150, seasons 200, identification 150, absence 200, return+coda 150 = 1000. Tight but doable.

Voice: first-person, precise, a little wry, unhurried. Avoid purple. Concrete nouns. Vary sentence lengths.

Names: give her none (narrator wouldn't know it); give the platform a particularity — the 7:12 to somewhere generic-real. Narrator gender unspecified-ish or default male? Keep neutral if possible naturally.

Song choice: "Moon River" recognizable, wistful. Hummed hums nicely (do-do-dum). Fine. Or avoid naming, have him identify it partially — "something old, big-band shaped" — but naming pays off better; recognition rewards reader. Moon River it is.

Draft mentally:

Open: "For three years I took the 7:12..." Set scene quickly. Her detail: coat the color of a school bus? Mustard wool coat. She stood at the far end by the trash can because — small mystery.

Humming: audible only in cold air when everything hushes? Nice logic: summer crowds masked it; autumn thinned; October, he heard it. Faint, looping, roughly sixteen bars then reset. Not quite keeping time — she swayed? No, keep simple.

Seasons/details: umbrella with one inverted rib; gloves mismatched (one red leather, one gray knit); she read MassMarket paperback thrillers with cracked spines, spine-cracker, pages bent back; she gave up her seat once to a man older than age itself; laughed once at phone, snorted, covered mouth. These accumulate the intimacy.

Near-contact: once, wind took her newspaper(?) — modernize: a receipt/ticket flew; he stamped it under boot, offered it; she said "thank you, sweetheart" — tiny, perfect. That single utterance proves she had a voice; before that she might have been silent film.

Identification arc: he Shazams air uselessly (comic beat: app listens to buses). Asks bandmate? No—keep solo. Realization arrives mid-shower or via old film on TV at mother's? Simplest: hears it drifting from an ice cream truck / elevator / dentist office muzak — bingo. "Moon River." Feels absurdly triumphant, tells no one, which is the joke and the sadness: it mattered like news.

Absence: mid-January. Monday gone—people skip days, fine. Tuesday. Wednesday, snow unmelted where she stood? No footprints isn't visible logic on platform... He notices her absence as a sound missing: platform "went mono." Weeks. Rationalizes: vacation, hospital, moved — none help; unnamed possibilities (the worst is left unsaid? implicit mortality — keep it hovering: "I found I had a list of explanations ranked from kind to true"). Oh, that's a good line. Keep.

His response: starts humming it himself at the platform, embarrassed, quiet — superstition, bait, vigil. Also notes others existed in her periphery as she was in his — nobody else glanced at her end of platform, meaning their connection existed nowhere outside his skull. "She was my secret in plain sight."

Return: third week of February or early spring. mustard coat. Thinner? Don't diagnose; readers will infer chemo if you say hat/scarf head coverings — do I want illness implied? Alternatives: she simply changed tunes. New melody he doesn't recognize — hers alone now. Maybe her hair shorter/scarf implies treatment — adds mortal stakes to earlier dread and release. I'll include one ambiguous physical note (a scarf in warm weather; she looked "edited") and resolve gently: she was back; that was all he got to know. He doesn't approach even now. Ends: sometimes across tracks, or final image—he still can't hear it when trains arrive, doors, PA — city noise reclaiming; last line something like: "It doesn't matter that I never knew her name. 'Moon River' has a second verse, and neither do most of us need the words."

Hmm last line needs craft. Options:
- "We were, I think, friends the way two keys on the same piano are related — struck by the same weather, resonant, never touching." Piano metaphor decent.
- Tie tempo: "Slower now. Spring was coming and she took her time." 
- Or end on him mouthing second verse he never learned.

Ending direction: closure without contact; gratitude for adjacency. Something like: "That's the arrangement I signed. Some people you get the whole of. Others you're issued a corner of—a coat, a hum—and the trick is not to demand the refund." Maybe too jokey late. Softer: final paragraph acknowledging all the medium-range beloveds; but keep meditation ≤3 sentences.

Also opening line candidates:
- "I want to tell you about the humming." (direct, hooks)
- "Every weekday for three years I stood at the same place on the same platform..."
Direct hook better.

Now compress into ~1000 actual words. I must count approximately as I finalize. Plan sections with rough budgets and write clean prose:

1. Opening scene/routine + her description (170)
2. Discovery of humming (140)
3. Seasonal catalog & the receipt exchange (220)
4. Identification: Moon River (160)
5. Absence & mourning-in-miniature (190)
6. Return + close (140)
Total ≈1020. Trim in final pass.

Format thoughts: This is creative writing — minimal formatting, no headers, maybe a title? A title is optional; a spare title could be nice: "Platform 4" or "Sixteen Bars" or "The Humming" or "Medium Range." "Sixteen Bars" evocative. I'll include a title in italics or bold? In chat, a bolded title line is fine. Keep prose in paragraphs, no lists obviously. Length ~1000 words as requested — user explicitly set the budget, honor it closely (within ~5%).

Write final now, carefully, aiming musicality.
